name: The Witch Tree (Manidoo-gizhigance / Spirit Little Cedar Tree)

location.address: On a rocky point on the Lake Superior shore, Grand Portage Indian Reservation, Grand Portage, Cook County, Minnesota
location.neighbourhood: Grand Portage (near Grand Portage National Monument / Grand Portage State Park)

access: Restricted, not a free walk-up. The Grand Portage Band closed the trail to independent public use in 1989 to protect the tree from vandalism; it may only be visited on a guided tour with a naturalist arranged through Grand Portage Lodge (218-475-2277). A guided hike to the tree was run as recently as 21 Feb 2024 (Heart of the Continent Partnership Winter Gathering, led by tribal member Travis Novitsky), which is also the most recent dated confirmation found that the tree still stands. Location is openly published by the tribe and multiple outlets, not withheld; the restriction is on unaccompanied access, not on knowledge of where it is.
transport: No public transit; reached by car via Grand Portage, MN near the Canadian border (~30 min north of Grand Marais), then by guided hike/boat from Grand Portage Lodge.
verify_notes: Sacred to the Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe (Manidoo-gizhigance, Spirit Little Cedar Tree). First European written record by French explorer Sieur de la Verendrye in 1731, who described it as already mature, giving a floor age of ~300 years then (~500 today per some tribal sources, kept broad here). Grows straight out of bare rock on the Lake Superior shoreline, gnarled, stunted and twisted from exposure; no girth figure found in sources checked. Traditionally offered tobacco by Ojibwe travellers for safe passage on the lake. Flagged because the most recent explicit alive-confirmation found is a Feb 2024 guided-hike listing rather than a dated survey or photo with visible health assessment; no death, storm-damage or removal report was found anywhere, and the site remains an actively promoted, actively guarded destination, which is itself evidence it still stands. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: yes, guided tours exist for exactly this purpose and it is a named stop on North Shore Minnesota tourism material. This is a single-tree destination in a remote location with no city in our published list within reach; treat as its own place (Grand Portage, MN) under the single-tree exception rather than folding into another city.

name: The Brandywine Sycamore (Lafayette Sycamore)

location.address: Beside the Gideon Gilpin House, Brandywine Battlefield Park, Baltimore Pike area, Chadds Ford, PA 19317
location.neighbourhood: Brandywine Battlefield Park, Chadds Ford Township, Delaware County

access: Free to view from the grounds; the Gideon Gilpin House itself is seen only on a timed guided tour (park operating as of 2023 visitor reviews, open Thu-Sun). The tree stands outside the house on the park grounds.
transport: No public transit found; car only. Roughly 40 km / 45-60 minutes by road from central Philadelphia, over the ~30-minute public-transport day-trip threshold, so this is its own place (Chadds Ford, PA) rather than folded into Philadelphia.
verify_notes: A witness-tree American sycamore at Brandywine Battlefield State Historic Site, standing beside the Gideon Gilpin farmhouse where the Marquis de Lafayette had his wounded leg dressed after the Battle of Brandywine, 11 Sept 1777. Per Union County College's tree-grove page (which grew a seed-grown descendant from this tree in 1997), the original was already 168 years old at the time of the 1777 battle, girth 220 inches (559 cm), height 111 ft (33.8 m), limb spread 60 ft; that puts a documented planting date around 1609 and a present age near 417 years, kept broad here. Also known from a 1987 National Arborist Association/ISA bicentennial marker at the site (photo in the batch: Bicentennial_tree_marker.jpg). Location precision is approximate: coordinates are the Gilpin House historical marker, not a tree-specific GPS fix, though the tree stands immediately beside that building so the margin is small (one yard). Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: borderline yes, it anchors visits to a National Historic Landmark battlefield with a specific, dressed-and-marked witness tree rather than being incidental scenery.

name: The Pinchot Sycamore

location.address: Pinchot Sycamore Park, Route 185 (Hopmeadow St / Simsbury Rd) on the east bank of the Farmington River, Simsbury, CT
location.neighbourhood: Simsbury, near the base of Talcott Mountain

access: Free, public town park (Pinchot Sycamore Park), open grounds with a boat launch onto the Farmington River; floodlit at night since a 1997 lighting project.
transport: No direct public transit found; car access off Route 185 south of Simsbury town center. Nearest published city is Boston or New York, both well over an hour away by road; treat as its own place (Simsbury, CT).
verify_notes: Connecticut state and national champion American sycamore, the largest tree in Connecticut, named for conservationist and CT governor Gifford Pinchot. Most recent measurement, Connecticut Notable Trees database, 27 Nov 2025: circumference 348 in (884 cm), height 99 ft (30.2 m), average spread 141 ft. Wikipedia estimates age at least 200, possibly over 300 years. An October 2011 snowstorm caused some canopy damage but the tree was not diminished and its large lower limbs remain intact; no death or major decline reported since. A dedicated town park exists around the tree with a boat launch and night floodlighting since 1997, strong evidence it is an established local landmark people already travel to. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: yes, it is promoted as the largest tree in the state and a named park exists purely around it.

name: The Sunderland Buttonball Tree
age_estimate: well over 350 years, possibly closer to 400
access: Free, stands on a public street (North Main Street) in the town center; a commemorative plaque was installed in front of it in 1987.
transport: No public transit found; roadside in Sunderland town center, car access. Roughly 15 km / 25 minutes by road north of Amherst; not close to any city on our published US list (nearest are Boston/New York, both 2+ hours). Treat as its own place (Sunderland, MA).
verify_notes: Widely called the largest tree in Massachusetts and reputedly the largest sycamore on the US East Coast ("the widest tree this side of the Mississippi", local saying). Wikipedia measurement, Nov 2019: girth 25 ft 8 in at 4.5 ft height (782 cm), height over 113 ft (34.4 m), spread 140 ft. Seeded before 1665 per tradition, giving an age well over 350 years, some estimates near 400; kept broad. Confirmed alive and current via an Amherst Indy arbor-spotlight article dated 3 April 2026 discussing the tree, plus a reader comment estimating its girth has grown to closer to 26 ft since the 2019 measurement (anecdotal, not used as a figure, but consistent with a living, actively growing, actively watched tree). A stone plaque near the tree notes it was already standing at the 1787 signing of the US Constitution. Roadside public landmark, one of the town's main tourist draws.

name: The Emancipation Oak

location.address: Hampton University campus, near the corner of E Queen St and Tyler St, Hampton, VA

access: Free, on the open grounds of Hampton University's campus; part of the university's National Historic Landmark district.
transport: Within Hampton, VA. Not one of our currently published US cities; treat as its own place (Hampton, VA) unless a future pass opens a Hampton Roads/Norfolk-Virginia Beach city page it could join.
verify_notes: Southern live oak on the Hampton University campus, canopy about 98 ft (30 m) in diameter, height roughly 50 ft (15.2 m). Named because in September 1863 the Virginia Peninsula's Black community gathered beneath it for the first Southern public reading of Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation; Mary Peake had already taught freed and enslaved children to read under the tree before the war. Part of the Hampton University NHL district, listed on the National Register of Historic Places 12 Nov 1969. Flagging on age: sources disagree substantially, from 150-200 years in older material to a 2023 estimate near 250 and a 2022 report near 309; no dendrochronology has been done (coring avoided to protect the tree), so treat any figure as an estimate rather than a measurement, kept broad here as roughly 200-300 years. Alive and current: active Yelp listing with reviews through August 2026, and the tree remains a functioning ceremonial site for Hampton University (Emancipation Day events, commencement-adjacent gatherings). Named one of National Geographic's Ten Great Trees of the World. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: yes, it is a National Historic Landmark element and a pilgrimage site tied to Reconstruction-era Black history.

name: The Dueling Oak

location.address: City Park, near where Dueling Oaks Drive meets Dreyfous Drive, between the Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden and the New Orleans Museum of Art, New Orleans, LA

access: Free, in a public City Park lawn area near the New Orleans Museum of Art.
transport: Within New Orleans, one of our published cities; check against nol_ prefixed trees already on the New Orleans page before this is written up, to avoid a duplicate entry.
verify_notes: The surviving half of a historic pair of live oaks under which duels were fought in the 19th century (dueling peaked 1834-1844, outlawed in the park in 1890); one of the pair was lost to a 1949 hurricane, this one survived both that storm and Hurricane Katrina in 2005 (City Park lost roughly 2,000 trees to Katrina, this was not one of them). Per uponarriving.com: approx. 70 ft tall (21.3 m), 25 ft girth (762 cm), estimated 300 years old. City Park's own site (neworleanscitypark.com) describes City Park as home to the world's largest collection of mature live oaks (about 800) and confirms the species as Quercus virginiana. A Yelp business listing for the tree shows reviews current to March 2026, further evidence it is an actively visited, standing landmark. Flagged because location_precision is approximate: sources describe the tree by nearby streets and landmarks (Dueling Oaks Drive/Dreyfous Drive, between the Besthoff Sculpture Garden and NOMA) rather than giving tree-specific GPS, and no fetched source gave exact coordinates; the lat/long here is an estimate of that intersection, not a confirmed pin. IMPORTANT: check this against New Orleans' already-published city file before adding, since New Orleans is already on our site (see rejected batch 3's note on the McDonogh Oak, another City Park tree already published as nol_001) and this may be a natural addition to the same page rather than its own place. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: borderline, it is one of the most storied individual trees in City Park's collection and a named stop in New Orleans tourism/history material, though it competes with many other named oaks in the same park.

name: The Devil's Tree

location.address: Mountain Road, Martinsville section of Bernards Township, Somerset County, NJ

access: Stands alone in an undeveloped field the township has designated as a public open space with posted opening hours (closes about half an hour after sunset per an on-site sign, since 2007). The field itself may be entered without asking anyone's permission, but the tree's own trunk is ringed by a chain-link fence, installed after repeated vandalism and midnight visits, so it is view-only rather than touchable up close.
transport: No public transit found; car access off Mountain Road, Martinsville, NJ. Not close to any of our published US cities (nearest large city is Newark/NYC area, well over an hour); treat as its own place (Bernards Township / Martinsville, NJ).
verify_notes: A solitary oak standing alone in an open field, locally famous as a haunted/cursed-tree legend (visitors report car trouble, unexplained warmth from the trunk, spontaneous scratches; treat all of this as folklore, not fact). Trunk shows old axe and chainsaw scarring from decades of vandalism and attempted removal/burning. Confirmed alive and standing as of a dated 2023 visit report (weirdnj.com). Fenced off since repeated vandalism, per an on-site 2007 sign giving public hours for the field. This is a distinct tree from the famous Basking Ridge White Oak (a different, 600-year-old specimen in the same general area that died in 2016 and was removed in 2017); do not conflate the two. Species not documented in any botanical survey found; described only as "an oak" with some dead limbs. Flag the species as unconfirmed and let the page ask the reader. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: yes, it is one of New Jersey's most visited local legends/haunted sites (named "most haunted place in NJ" by Patch.com) and draws visitors purely for the tree and its story.

name: The Great White Oak of Logan (Logan Oak)

location.address: Old Logan Cemetery, northeast corner, near the junction of Keynes Drive and North Mulberry Street, Logan, OH
location.neighbourhood: North side of Logan, Hocking County

access: Free, on the grounds of a public cemetery (Old Logan Cemetery); described by a visiting naturalist as easy to find, with respectful visitors welcome.
transport: No public transit found; car access in Logan, OH (Hocking County). Not close to any of our published US cities; treat as its own place (Logan, OH), roughly an hour southeast of Columbus.
verify_notes: A large, ornate white oak on the grounds of Old Logan Cemetery, described by an Ohio naturalist (jimmccormac.blogspot.com, Sept 2019, an hour spent documenting it from multiple angles) as 'easily the largest and most ornate' white oak he had seen, with huge gnarled limbs radiating from a substantial trunk. Said to be about 600 years old; reportedly age-checked by the Ohio Department of Natural Resources roughly 30 years ago, though the exact method is not documented in sources found, so kept as a broad estimate. Featured on College Jeopardy in 2022. The local Tree Commission collects its acorns and grows them into saplings sold as a fundraiser to carry on its legacy, which is both an active local ecological/civic program and indirect evidence the parent tree is alive and being maintained as of the program's most recent activity. Flagged because no explicit recent (post-2022) health confirmation was found and no girth/height measurement was found in sources checked. Location precision is approximate: no tree-specific coordinates were found, only a cemetery and cross-street description; the lat/long given is an estimate of that area, not a confirmed pin. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: yes, it is Hocking County's best-known individual tree and a regional record-age white oak with an active local preservation programme built around it.
